lessons.title: Make a monthly budget
lessons.goal: I can talk about my monthly budget and say what I spend.

newItems.definition: Money you get for your work.
Money you spend on something.
To make a plan for your money.
newItems.example: Set a budget for the month.

newItems.definition: To follow your money plan.
To know how much you spend.

mainWord.definition: Money you get for your work.

lessons.mainWordForms: Income is a noun. Income means money you get for your work. My income is $3,000 a month.
lessons.expression: I set a budget every month.
lessons.use: Use this to talk about your money plan.
lessons.expressionTask: Sam makes a plan for his money. What does he do every month?
lessons.grammar: Present simple for habits: I spend $500 on food every month
lessons.pattern: I spend $500 on food every month.
lessons.example: I spend $500 on food every month.
context: Sam makes a plan for his money every month.
I set a budget every month. I keep track of my money.
dialogue: Sam, do you set a budget every month?
Yes, I set a budget every month. My income is $3,000 a month.
What is your biggest expense?
Food is a big expense. I spend $500 on food every month.
Do you stick to a budget?
Yes, I stick to a budget. I keep track of my money every week.
lessons.listening: Sam sets a budget every month. His income is $3,000 a month. Food is a big expense. He spends $500 on food every month. Sam sticks to a budget. He keeps track of his money every week. At the end of the month, Sam is happy. He has money left.
lessons.question: What is Sam's biggest expense?
lessons.reading: Sam works at an office in the city. Every month, he gets his income. His income is $3,000 a month. Sam sets a budget every month. He writes down his money plan. Food is a big expense. Sam spends $500 on food every month. He also spends money on his car, his house, and his phone. Sam sticks to a budget. He keeps track of his money every week. He writes down every price in a small book. At the end of the month, Sam looks at his book. He is happy. He has money left. Sam says, 'I set a budget every month, and I stick to a budget. I keep track of my money. That is my plan.'
lessons.readingQ: What does Sam do every month?
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about your monthly budget. What is your income? What is your biggest expense? Do you stick to a budget?
lessons.speakingSample: I set a budget every month. My income is $3,000 a month. Food is a big expense. I spend $500 on food every month. I also spend money on my car and my house. I stick to a budget. I keep track of my money every week. At the end of the month, I am happy. I have money left.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend about your monthly budget. Say what your income is and what your biggest expense is.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Tom, I want to tell you about my monthly budget. My income is $3,000 a month. I set a budget every month. Food is a big expense. I spend $500 on food every month. I also spend money on my car and my house. I stick to a budget. I keep track of my money every week. At the end of the month, I am happy. I have money left. Best, Sam
lessons.sound: Income has its strongest beat on IN. In income, say IN clearly at the start. In expense, say PENSE clearly at the end.
lessons.wordSample: Food is a big expense. He spends $500 on food every month.

lessons.title: Save for something special
lessons.goal: I can talk about saving money for something special.

newItems.definition: A lot of money.
Having a lot of money.
To keep money until you can buy something.
newItems.example: I save up for a car.

newItems.definition: To keep money for later.
To keep money for a hard time later.

lessons.mainWordForms: Fortune is a noun. Fortune means a lot of money. He made a fortune.
lessons.expression: I save up for a new car.
lessons.use: Use this to talk about saving money for something you want.
lessons.expressionTask: Sam wants a new car. What does he do?
lessons.grammar: will for plans: I will save $100 every month
context: I save up for a new car. I put money aside every month.
dialogue: Sam, do you want a new car?
Yes, I save up for a new car. I put money aside every month.
How much do you save every month?
I save $100 every month. I will save for two years.
Do you want to be wealthy?
No, I do not need a fortune. I save for a rainy day.
lessons.listening: Sam wants a new car. He saves up for a new car. He puts money aside every month. He saves $100 every month. He will save for two years. Sam does not need a fortune. He is not wealthy, but he is happy. At the end of two years, Sam will buy a new car.
lessons.question: How much does Sam save every month?
lessons.reading: Sam wants a new car. He saves up for a new car. He puts money aside every month. He saves $100 every month. He will save for two years. Sam does not need a fortune. He is not wealthy, but he is happy. Sam saves for a rainy day. He keeps money in the bank for a hard time later. His family helps him. His family puts money aside, too. At the end of two years, Sam will buy a new car. He says, 'I save up for a new car. I put money aside every month. I save for a rainy day.' Sam is happy. His new car will be red.
lessons.readingQ: How much does Sam save every month?
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about saving money. What do you save up for? How much do you save every month? Do you save for a rainy day?
lessons.speakingSample: I save up for a new car. I put money aside every month. I save $100 every month. I will save for two years. I do not need a fortune. I am not wealthy, but I am happy. I save for a rainy day. At the end of two years, I will buy a new car. My family is happy.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend about saving money. Say what you save up for and how much you save every month.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Lisa, I want to tell you about saving money. I save up for a new car. I put money aside every month. I save $100 every month. I will save for two years. I do not need a fortune. I am not wealthy, but I am happy. I save for a rainy day. At the end of two years, I will buy a new car. My family is happy, too. Best, Sam
lessons.sound: Fortune has its strongest beat on FOR. In fortune, say FOR clearly at the start. In wealthy, say WEAL clearly at the start.
lessons.wordTask: How much does Sam save every month?
lessons.wordSample: He saves $100 every month. He will save for two years.

lessons.title: Compare prices before you buy
lessons.goal: I can compare prices and talk about a good deal.

newItems.definition: Fair; not too high in price.
Used before by someone else.
A good price for something.
To look at prices in different shops.
A very good price for something.

mainWord.definition: Fair; not too high in price.

lessons.mainWordForms: Reasonable is an adjective. Reasonable means fair; not too high in price. The price is reasonable.
lessons.use: Use this to say the price is good.
lessons.expressionTask: Sam finds shoes for a low price. What does he say?
lessons.grammar: Comparatives: This shop is cheaper than that shop
lessons.pattern: This shop is cheaper than that shop.
lessons.task: This shop is cheaper than that ___.
lessons.example: This shop is cheaper than that shop.
context: Sam looks at shoes in two shops.
This is a good deal. The price is reasonable.
dialogue: Sam, do you like these shoes?
Yes, and this is a good deal. The price is reasonable.
Did you shop around?
Yes, I shopped around. I looked at three shops.
Is this a steal?
Yes, it is a steal. Secondhand shoes are cheap, too.
lessons.listening: Sam wants new shoes. He shops around. He looks at three shops. In the first shop, the shoes are $100. In the second shop, the shoes are $80. This is a good deal. The price is reasonable. It is a steal. Sam buys the shoes. He is happy. Secondhand shoes are cheap, too.
lessons.question: How much are the shoes in the second shop?
lessons.reading: Sam wants new shoes. He shops around before he buys. He looks at shoes in three shops. In the first shop, the shoes are $100. In the second shop, the shoes are $80. In the third shop, the shoes are $50. Sam says, 'This is a good deal. The price is reasonable.' It is a steal. Sam buys the shoes. He is happy. Sam likes to shop around. He looks at the market, too. Secondhand shoes are cheap. Sam buys secondhand books at the market. He says, 'I shop around before I buy. A good deal makes me happy.' Sam tells his friend Tom about the shoes. Tom is happy for Sam. Tom says, 'You found a good deal.'
lessons.readingQ: How much are the shoes in the third shop?
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about comparing prices. What do you want to buy? Do you shop around? Is the price reasonable?
lessons.speakingSample: I want new shoes. I shop around before I buy. I look at shoes in three shops. In the first shop, the shoes are $100. In the second shop, the shoes are $80. This is a good deal. The price is reasonable. It is a steal. I buy the shoes. I am happy.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend about comparing prices. Say what you want to buy and how much it costs in two shops.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Tom, I want to tell you about comparing prices. I want new shoes. I shop around before I buy. I look at shoes in three shops. In the first shop, the shoes are $100. In the second shop, the shoes are $80. This is a good deal. The price is reasonable. It is a steal. I buy the shoes. I am happy. Secondhand shoes are cheap, too. Best, Sam
lessons.sound: Reasonable has its strongest beat on REA. In reasonable, say REA clearly at the start. In secondhand, say SEC clearly at the start.
lessons.wordTask: How much are the shoes in the second shop?
lessons.wordSample: The shoes are $80. This is a good deal.

lessons.title: Pay for things
lessons.goal: I can talk about paying for things.

newItems.definition: Money you pay.
The price of a bus or train trip.
To pay the money you owe.
To put numbers together.
To find out how much something costs.

lessons.mainWordForms: Payment is a noun. Payment means money you pay. The payment is due.
lessons.use: Use this to say you pay the money you owe.
lessons.expressionTask: Sam eats lunch at a restaurant. What does he do?
lessons.grammar: Past simple for shopping: I paid the bill yesterday
context: Sam eats lunch at a restaurant with Anna.
I pay the bill. The payment is $20.
dialogue: Sam, did you eat lunch at the restaurant?
Yes, I ate lunch with Anna. I pay the bill.
How much is the payment?
The payment is $20. The bus fare is $2.
Do you work out the cost first?
Yes, I add up the costs. I work out the cost before I buy.
lessons.listening: Sam eats lunch at a restaurant with Anna. The payment is $20. Sam pays the bill. Anna pays the bus fare. The bus fare is $2. Sam adds up the costs. He works out the cost before he buys. Sam and Anna drink coffee. The coffee is $4. Sam is happy.
lessons.question: How much is the payment for lunch?
lessons.reading: Sam eats lunch at a restaurant with Anna. The payment is $20. Sam pays the bill. Anna pays the bus fare. The bus fare is $2. Sam adds up the costs. He works out the cost before he buys. Sam likes lunch with Anna. They drink coffee. The coffee is $4. Sam says, 'I pay the bill. I add up the costs. I work out the cost before I buy.' Anna is happy. She says, 'The bus fare is $2. The train fare is $3.' Sam and Anna take the bus home. Sam says, 'The payment is $20. The coffee is $4. Lunch is good.' Anna says, 'Thank you, Sam. Lunch is good.' Sam is happy.
lessons.readingQ: How much is the bus fare?
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about paying for lunch. How much is the payment? Who pays the bill? What is the bus fare?
lessons.speakingSample: I eat lunch at a restaurant with Anna. The payment is $20. I pay the bill. Anna pays the bus fare. The bus fare is $2. I add up the costs. I work out the cost before I buy. We drink coffee. The coffee is $4. I am happy. I like lunch with Anna.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend about paying for lunch. Say how much the payment is and who pays the bill.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Lisa, I want to tell you about lunch. I eat lunch at a restaurant with Anna. The payment is $20. I pay the bill. Anna pays the bus fare. The bus fare is $2. I add up the costs. I work out the cost before I buy. We drink coffee. The coffee is $4. I am happy. I like lunch with Anna. Best, Sam
lessons.sound: Payment has its strongest beat on PAY. In payment, say PAY clearly at the start. In fare, say FARE clearly.
lessons.wordTask: How much is the bus fare?
lessons.wordSample: The bus fare is $2. Anna pays the bus fare.

lessons.title: Borrow money
lessons.goal: I can talk about borrowing money.

newItems.definition: Money you must pay back.
Money you borrow from a bank.
Extra money you pay for a loan.
To borrow money from a bank.
To give back money you borrowed.

lessons.mainWordForms: Debt is a noun. Debt means money you must pay back. He has a big debt.
lessons.use: Use this to say you give back money you borrowed.
lessons.expressionTask: Tom borrows money from the bank. What does he do every month?
lessons.grammar: First conditional: If I borrow money, I will pay it back
lessons.pattern: If I borrow money, I will pay it back.
lessons.task: If I borrow money, I will pay it ___.
lessons.example: If I borrow money, I will pay it back.
context: Tom takes out a loan from the bank.
I pay back the loan. The interest is $50 a month.
dialogue: Tom, did you take out a loan?
Yes, I took out a loan from the bank. The loan is $5,000.
How much is the interest?
The interest is $50 a month. I pay back the loan every month.
Do you have a big debt?
Yes, I have a big debt, but I pay back the loan every month.
lessons.listening: Tom takes out a loan from the bank. The loan is $5,000. The interest is $50 a month. Tom pays back the loan every month. He has a big debt. Tom calls his friend Sam for help. Sam says, 'Do not worry. Pay back the loan every month.' He pays back the loan.
lessons.question: How much is the interest every month?
lessons.reading: Tom takes out a loan from the bank. The loan is $5,000. The interest is $50 a month. Tom pays back the loan every month. He has a big debt. Tom calls his friend Sam for help. Sam says, 'Do not worry. Pay back the loan every month.' Tom writes a letter to the bank. He says, 'I take out a loan. I pay back the loan every month. The interest is $50 a month.' The bank is happy. Tom is happy. He says, 'I have a big debt, but I pay back the loan. I take out a loan, and I pay it back.' Sam helps Tom. Sam is a good friend. Tom thanks Sam.
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about borrowing money. Did you take out a loan? How much is the interest? How do you pay it back?
lessons.speakingSample: I take out a loan from the bank. The loan is $5,000. The interest is $50 a month. I pay back the loan every month. I have a big debt. I call my friend Sam for help. Sam says, 'Do not worry. Pay back the loan every month.' I am happy.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend about borrowing money. Say how much the loan is and how much the interest is every month.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Tom, I want to tell you about my loan. I take out a loan from the bank. The loan is $5,000. The interest is $50 a month. I pay back the loan every month. I have a big debt. I call my friend Sam for help. Sam says, 'Do not worry. Pay back the loan every month.' I am happy. Thank you for your help. Best, Sam
lessons.sound: Debt has one strong beat. Say DEBT clearly. In loan, say LOAN clearly.
lessons.wordSample: The loan is $5,000. The interest is $50 a month.

lessons.title: Make a big money choice
lessons.goal: I can talk about a big money choice.

newItems.definition: To put money into something to make more money.
Money you make after you pay the costs.
To need to pay money back.
Worth all the money you pay.
To cost too much money.
newItems.example: It will not break the bank.

mainWord.definition: To put money into something to make more money.

lessons.mainWordForms: Invest is a verb. Invest means to put money into something to make more money. I invest in Apple.
lessons.use: Use this to say something is worth all the money you pay.
lessons.expressionTask: Sam buys a good computer. What does he say about it?
lessons.grammar: should for advice: You should invest your money
context: Sam buys a new computer for his business.
It is worth every penny. It will not break the bank.
dialogue: Sam, did you buy a new computer?
Yes, I bought a new computer for my business. It is worth every penny.
Did it break the bank?
No, it will not break the bank. I invest my money well.
Do you owe money for the computer?
No, I do not owe money. I pay for it today.
lessons.listening: Sam buys a new computer for his business. It is worth every penny. It will not break the bank. Sam invests his money well. He does not owe money for the computer. He pays for it today. Sam likes his new computer. He uses it every day. Sam is happy.
lessons.question: What does Sam buy for his business?
lessons.reading: Sam buys a new computer for his business. It is worth every penny. It will not break the bank. Sam invests his money well. He does not owe money for the computer. He pays for it today. Sam likes his new computer. He uses it every day. His business is good. The shop makes a profit. Sam says, 'I invest my money well. It is worth every penny.' Anna asks, 'Do you owe money for the computer?' Sam says, 'No, I do not owe money. It will not break the bank.' Sam is happy. He has a good plan for the future. Sam tells his friend Tom about the computer. Tom is happy for Sam. Tom says, 'That is a good plan.'
lessons.readingQ: Does Sam owe money for the computer?
lessons.speaking: Tell a friend about a big money choice. What did you buy? Is it worth every penny? Did it break the bank?
lessons.speakingSample: I buy a new computer for my business. It is worth every penny. It will not break the bank. I invest my money well. I do not owe money for the computer. I pay for it today. I like my new computer. I use it every day. I am happy.
lessons.writing: Write a short email to a friend about a big money choice. Say what you bought and if it is worth every penny.
lessons.writingSample: Dear Tom, I want to tell you about a big money choice. I buy a new computer for my business. It is worth every penny. It will not break the bank. I invest my money well. I do not owe money for the computer. I pay for it today. I like my new computer. I use it every day. I am happy. It is a good plan for the future. Best, Sam
lessons.sound: Invest has its strongest beat on VEST. In invest, say VEST clearly at the end. In profit, say PROF clearly at the start.
lessons.wordTask: What does Sam buy for his business?

lessons.title: Live within your means
lessons.goal: I can talk about living within my means.

newItems.definition: Money you pay to the government.
The money of a country.
newItems.example: The currency here is the dollar.

newItems.definition: Not having enough money.
To have just enough money to live.
newItems.example: It is hard to make ends meet.

newItems.definition: To spend no more money than you have.

mainWord.definition: Money you pay to the government.

lessons.mainWordForms: Tax is a noun. Tax means money you pay to the government. We pay tax every year.
lessons.use: Use this to say you spend no more money than you have.
lessons.expressionTask: Sam plans a trip to London. What does he say about money?
lessons.grammar: going to for plans: I am going to pay my tax in April
lessons.pattern: I am going to pay my tax in April.
lessons.task: I am going to pay my tax in ___.
lessons.example: I am going to pay my tax in April.
context: Sam plans a trip to London.
Live within your means. The currency in London is the pound.
dialogue: Sam, do you plan a trip to London?
Yes, I plan a trip to London. The currency in London is the pound.
Do you pay tax every year?
Yes, I pay tax every year. I am going to pay my tax in April.
Is it hard to make ends meet?
Sometimes it is hard to make ends meet, but I live within my means.
lessons.listening: Sam plans a trip to London. The currency in London is the pound. Sam pays tax every year. He is going to pay his tax in April. Sometimes it is hard to make ends meet, but Sam lives within his means. Sam reads about poverty in the news.

lessons.readingQ: What is the currency in London?

lessons.wordTask: What is the currency in London?

lessons.goal: I can use money English in a new situation.

newItems.definition: Money you get for work, usually every week.
Every year.
Money for a special purpose.
To use or spend less of something.
To see how much money is in your account.

lessons.mainWordForms: Wage is a noun. Wage means money you get for work, usually every week. His wage is $20 an hour.
